notes.title: Zero vectors and angle endpoints
notes.text: The sign rules for an angle require both vectors to be nonzero. A positive dot product also includes the case of the same direction, angle $0^\circ$.
notes.write: A zero vector has zero dot product with every vector but no defined direction or angle.

notes.title: Normal to the plane
notes.text: For nonparallel three-dimensional vectors, the nonzero cross product is perpendicular to the plane they span, not a vector lying in that plane. Parallel vectors have zero cross product, which does not determine a unique unit normal.
notes.write: Check perpendicularity by taking the dot product with each original vector.

ican.text: I can calculate a dot product, find an angle between nonzero vectors and test perpendicularity.
I can distinguish the directed vector angle from the acute angle between lines.
I can calculate a cross product in three dimensions, interpret its orientation and verify it is perpendicular to both vectors.
I can use the cross-product magnitude for parallelogram and triangle areas.
I can find signed scalar and vector projections and the magnitude of a perpendicular component.

ku.text: For $\mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $\mathbf v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, the scalar product is $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3$. The result is a scalar.
For nonzero vectors, $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta$, where $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$ is the angle between their directions. Divide by the magnitudes and use inverse cosine.

For nonzero vectors, a zero dot product means perpendicular directions. A positive product means an angle less than $90^\circ$, including $0^\circ$; a negative product means an angle greater than $90^\circ$, including $180^\circ$. A zero vector has no defined angle.

Lines have no preferred direction. The smaller angle between two lines with nonzero direction vectors satisfies $\cos\phi=|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|/(|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|)$, where $0\leq\phi\leq90^\circ$.
The three-dimensional cross product is $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\;u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\;u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$. It is a vector perpendicular to both inputs.

For nonparallel nonzero vectors, the right-hand rule chooses its direction and $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\sin\theta$. Reversing the order changes its sign. If the vectors are parallel or either is zero, the product is zero and it does not define a unit normal.

The magnitude of the cross product is the area of the parallelogram generated by the two vectors; half of it is the area of the corresponding triangle. Area is nonnegative and has square units when the vectors are lengths.

For $\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0$, the signed scalar component of $\mathbf u$ in the direction of $\mathbf v$ is $(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)/|\mathbf v|$. A negative value means the component points opposite the chosen direction.

The vector projection of $\mathbf u$ onto $\mathbf v$ is $\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|^2}\mathbf v$. Subtract it from $\mathbf u$ to obtain the perpendicular component vector.

The magnitude of the perpendicular component is $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|/|\mathbf v|$ in three dimensions. A unit normal to the plane is $(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)/|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|$ only when the cross product is nonzero.

terms.text: The dot product, a scalar obtained from two vectors.
The cross product, a three-dimensional vector perpendicular to both inputs.
A vector of magnitude one perpendicular to a specified plane; its orientation must be stated.
The signed magnitude of a vector along a chosen direction.
The vector part of one vector parallel to another.
The smaller angle between their directions, independent of which way each direction vector is chosen.

formula.text: Dot product: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum u_iv_i=|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta$ for nonzero vectors.
Cross-product magnitude: $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|=|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\sin\theta$.

For $\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0$, the signed scalar component of $\mathbf u$ along $\mathbf v$ is $(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)/|\mathbf v|$; the perpendicular component magnitude is $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|/|\mathbf v|$.

worked.prompt: Two sides of a parallelogram are represented by $\mathbf u=(2,1,2)$ m and $\mathbf v=(1,2,2)$ m, with their tails at the same point.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the scalar product and the angle between the vectors.
parts.a: $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=2(1)+1(2)+2(2)=8$. Both magnitudes are $3$ m, so $\cos\theta=8/9$ and $\theta=\cos^{-1}(8/9)\approx27.3^\circ$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$ and verify that it is perpendicular to both vectors.
parts.a: $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(1(2)-2(2),2(1)-2(2),2(2)-1(1))=(-2,-2,3)$. Its dot products with $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ are both $0$, verifying perpendicularity.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find the parallelogram area and the area of a triangle formed by these sides.
parts.a: The product has magnitude $\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-2)^2+3^2}=\sqrt{17}$. The parallelogram area is $\sqrt{17}\text{ m}^2$ and the triangle area is $\sqrt{17}/2\text{ m}^2$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Find the signed scalar component and vector projection of $\mathbf u$ in the direction of $\mathbf v$.
parts.a: The scalar component is $8/|\mathbf v|=8/3$ m. The vector projection is $\frac{8}{9}(1,2,2)$ m. The scalar and the vector answer describe different quantities.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Find the magnitude of the component of $\mathbf u$ perpendicular to $\mathbf v$ and a unit normal in the direction of $\mathbf u\times\mathbf v$.
parts.a: The perpendicular component magnitude is $|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v|/|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{17}/3$ m. The requested unit normal is $(-2,-2,3)/\sqrt{17}$. Reversing the cross-product order would reverse this normal.

parts.label: f
parts.q: Find the angle between the lines directed by $\mathbf u$ and $-\mathbf v$.
parts.a: The angle between the chosen directed vectors is about $152.7^\circ$, but a line has no preferred direction. The smaller angle between the lines is therefore $180^\circ-152.7^\circ\approx27.3^\circ$.

kq.q: Why does a zero dot product indicate perpendicularity only for nonzero vectors?
kq.model: The angle formula requires defined directions and nonzero magnitudes. The zero vector gives a zero product but has no defined angle.

kq.q: Why does swapping the cross-product order reverse the result?
kq.model: The right-hand-rule orientation reverses when the ordered pair is reversed; the magnitude remains the same.

kq.q: Why is a triangle’s area half the cross-product magnitude?
kq.model: The magnitude gives the base times perpendicular height of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors. A matching triangle occupies half of it.

kq.q: Why can the scalar component be negative?
kq.model: It records signed amount along the chosen direction. A negative component points opposite that direction; its magnitude is nonnegative.
